opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I get a lot, and I think it's a really fair one. My short answer is that LLMs are great tools, but they work best when you understand what they're doing. If you don't have the fundamentals, it's very hard to tell when the model is giving you something subtly wrong, and with math and code, subtly wrong can be worse than obviously wrong.

I often compare it to calculators. We've had calculators for decades, but we still teach kids arithmetic, because it builds intuition. You need a feel for whether a number makes sense. It's the same with coding. If an LLM writes a training loop and forgets to zero the gradients, or there's some off-by-one issue in the attention mask, it'll probably still run. It just won't do what you want, and you won't notice unless you know what to look for.

There's also a personal side for me. Coding things from scratch is how I learn. When I implemented an LLM from the ground up for my book, I understood things I'd only had a vague sense of from reading papers, like how the KV cache works or why certain normalization choices matter. If I'd just had a model generate that code, I'd have a working artifact, but not the understanding. And that understanding is what lets you go further: debugging, trying new ideas, reading research critically.

So I'd frame it this way: LLMs raise the floor, so you can get started faster, but understanding the math and code raises the ceiling. And I think people who combine the two, who use LLMs as a productivity tool but actually know what's under the hood, are the ones who'll get the most out of these tools. Honestly, it's also just fun. There's a real satisfaction in building something and understanding why it works.

r001.rationale: The response says coding knowledge helps identify bugs and debug LLM-generated code, but it does not state that correcting the implementation directly is more efficient than repeatedly prompting the LLM.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get a lot, and I think the answer is actually pretty simple: you can't evaluate what you can't understand. An LLM can write the code for me, sure, and it can walk me through a derivation. But when it makes a mistake, and it does make mistakes, often subtle ones, I need to be able to catch that. If I'm just copying and pasting outputs that I can't verify, I'm not really doing the work anymore. I'm just a relay.

There's also something about the learning process itself. The reason I write things from scratch in my books, implementing attention, implementing the training loop, isn't because I think people should hand-code these things in production. It's that the act of building it is what forms the mental model. You can read about how a transformer works a hundred times, but until you've actually wired up the matrices yourself and seen the shapes line up, or not line up, it doesn't really click. And the LLM doing that for you robs you of exactly the part that produces understanding.

The analogy I like is calculators. We've had calculators for decades, and we still teach arithmetic. Not because anyone expects you to do long division by hand at work, but because without that foundation you can't reason about numbers at all. You wouldn't notice if the calculator gave you something off by a factor of ten. Math and coding are the same thing for machine learning. They're the foundation that lets you have intuitions, ask the right questions, and spot when something is wrong.

And honestly, I think the people who benefit most from these tools are the ones who already know the material well. If you understand what you're asking for, an LLM makes you dramatically faster. If you don't, it mostly makes you confidently wrong at scale. So the tools raise the ceiling for people with fundamentals, but they don't remove the need for fundamentals. If anything, they make them more valuable, because now the skill that matters is judgment, and judgment comes from having done the thing yourself.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s still worthwhile because getting an answer and understanding an answer are two different things. An LLM can write code for you, but you still have to decide: Is this solving the right problem? Is the result reasonable? And if something goes wrong, how do you figure out why?

For that, you need some foundation. You don’t necessarily have to do every calculation by hand, but understanding the math helps you ask better questions and evaluate what you get back. With coding, it’s similar. It’s often easy to produce something that runs. It’s harder to know whether it does what you intended.

And I think there’s a learning aspect we shouldn’t skip. When you work through a problem yourself, you build intuition. If you always outsource that process, you might get the immediate task done, but you haven’t developed the understanding that helps with the next problem.

So I would use LLMs as part of learning. Ask for a hint, ask for an explanation, compare their solution with yours. These tools can make learning much more accessible. But knowing math and coding makes you better at using them, too.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it comes down to being able to judge what you get back. An LLM can write code for you, but you still need to understand whether that code solves the problem you actually have. Does it make the right assumptions? How would you test it? If something goes wrong, can you figure out why?

And with math, the value isn’t just being able to do a calculation by hand. It’s developing an intuition for how things work. If you understand the underlying concepts, you can ask better questions and recognize when an answer doesn’t make sense.

So I think these tools can change how we learn. You can use an LLM to explain a difficult concept, give you examples, or help you get past a coding error. But there’s a difference between getting a solution and understanding a solution. I would still encourage people to work through problems themselves, because that’s how you build the understanding that makes the tool more useful.
